title: A conceptual framework for identity updating and symbolic processing in high-acuity counseling
abstract: Abstract Psychotherapy contains multiple well-developed accounts of affect regulation, mental imagery, cognitive and narrative meaning-making, behavioral enactment, and autobiographical identity. Further conceptual work is nevertheless needed to specify how these processes may interact recursively during identity-related therapeutic change, particularly in periods of high affective activation. This paper presents the Recursive Identity Stabilization Engine (RISE) and the associated ERCA protocol (Externalize, Rename, Contain, Anchor) as an integrated, hypothesis-generating conceptual and procedural framework. RISE organizes identity-related processing across six functionally distinguishable but non-linear processes: Affective Activation (A), Symbolic Representation/Translation (S), Meaning (M), Narrative Integration (N), Behavioral Enactment (B), and Feedback (F). Feedback refers to perceived internal and environmental consequences following enactment and may include expectancy-confirming information, discrepant or expectancy-disconfirming information, social response, and other interpreted consequences that influence subsequent processing. ERCA provides a corresponding set of clinical moves for working with affectively charged symbolic material; these moves are proposed to operate across multiple RISE processes rather than constituting a fixed one-to-one sequence. The framework draws upon research in mental imagery and imagery rescripting [1–3], narrative identity and autobiographical reasoning [4, 5], narrative externalization [6], process-based psychotherapy [7, 8], and qualified accounts of memory updating and reconsolidation-like processes [9, 10]. RISE–ERCA is not presented as an empirically validated treatment model or established causal mechanism. Rather, it specifies a testable process architecture, delineates its relationship to established therapeutic approaches, identifies clinical scope and safety boundaries, and proposes directions for subsequent empirical evaluation. A central proposition is that immediate changes in symbolic representation or meaning should be distinguished from their subsequent propagation into narrative integration, behavioral enactment, and recursive stabilization.
